title: The misplaced anchor: interest rate components in perpetual futures funding mechanisms
items.abstract: <jats:p>Futures contracts derive their fair price from the cost of carry - the net expense of holding the underlying asset until delivery. In TradFi, this cost is embedded directly in the futures price through the basis, which converges to zero at expiry via arbitrage. Perpetual futures, having no expiry, replace this convergence mechanism with a periodic funding rate. The standard funding rate formula, established by BitMEX in 2016, includes two components: a premium index that ties the perp price to spot, and an interest rate (IR) component that captures the cost of carry as a baseline payment from one side to the other. This paper traces the IR component from its theoretical roots in cost-of-carry pricing, through its implementation history - from the original dynamic rate sourced from Bitfinex lending markets to its entrenchment as a fixed 0.01% per 8 hours (~10.95% APR) in April 2017, and its subsequent, largely unquestioned adoption as the industry standard across centralized and decentralized exchanges. We evaluate this fixed anchor in light of prevailing capital costs observed in DeFi lending platforms, highlighting the mismatches and persistent structural distortions that emerge when the IR departs from the real cost of financing. We detail cases where specific exchanges have intentionally modified the IR for certain markets, and articulate criteria for a more principled calibration. Finally, we critically examine the standard funding rate formula employed by most exchanges, showing how both its structure and its embedded anchors can generate systematic mispricings and unintended market consequences.</jats:p>

title: Hyperbolic Funding Rate Mechanisms for Open Interest Balancing in Perpetual Futures Markets
items.abstract: <jats:p>Funding rate mechanisms are the primary microstructure tool used to balance long and short open interest in perpetual futures markets. Despite their central role, most centralized and decentralized venues rely on linear or near-linear funding rules, and systematic analysis of non-linear alternatives remains limited. I introduce and analyze a class of hyperbolic funding rate mechanisms that are capacity-aware by construction: they impose weak incentives near equilibrium while imposing sharply increasing marginal costs as open interest imbalance approaches protocol capacity constraints. I provide an axiomatic derivation showing the hyperbolic form is the unique mechanism satisfying four natural desiderata: linearity near equilibrium, capacity awareness, monotonicity, and convexity with a simple pole. I embed the mechanism in a mean-field game model and establish existence and uniqueness of equilibrium under standard conditions. Lyapunov stability analysis provides sufficient conditions for asymptotic rebalancing and characterizes the oscillation boundary. Agent-based simulations with 100 heterogeneous traders across four behavioral classes show that hyperbolic funding reduces open interest rebalancing half-life by 10-70% relative to linear funding under severe shocks, defined as initial imbalance greater than 50% of protocol capacity, while maintaining identical behavior near equilibrium. Monte Carlo analysis over 100 randomized shock scenarios confirms robustness. I characterize welfare redistribution across trader classes and identify the oscillation failure mode with explicit parameter bounds. I provide a parameter selection framework for protocol designers.</jats:p>

title: A Cross-venue Data Dictionary for Perpetual Futures: Funding-rate Mechanisms, Pre-Trade Rules, and Measurement Error across 21 Exchanges
items.abstract: <jats:p>Cross-venue perpetual-futures analysis often treats a funding rate as a directly comparable scalar. We test that premise using official documentation and read-only public interfaces for 21 centralized and on-chain venues. We construct a dated data dictionary covering funding formulas, settlement schedules, caps, field semantics, clock and rate units, open-interest and turnover bases, fees, liquidation backstops, and pre-trade rules. Fifteen venues share a clamped interest-minus-premium core, but three use distinct formula structures and three require separate treatment. Instrument-level intervals invalidate an exchange-wide eight-hour assumption: Gate’s 1,070 rows on 3 November 2026 contain 420 four-hour contracts, while GRVT and Variational also return multiple intervals. A new sample of 1,840 public history rows shows median absolute timestamp offsets from the nearest hour of 36 ms at Hyperliquid, 937 ms at Extended, and 3,680 ms at Pacifica; all 100 edgeX records are exact. Deterministic examples show 100-fold unit errors, twofold annualization errors, and fee differences exceeding one typical funding payment. The results provide a reproducible normalization layer for funding-rate and execution-cost measurement, not evidence of trading profitability.</jats:p>

title: Failure of Cross-Sectional Alpha Screening on Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures: A Quantitative Post-Mortem Using OHLCV and Funding Rate Signals
items.abstract: <jats:p>This study constructs and evaluates three composite alpha screening models-naive linear, orthogonal linear, and XGBoost ranker-for long-short cross-sectional portfolios on ten USDT-margined perpetual futures contracts traded on Binance. The signal set draws from daily and intraday price, volume, and funding rate data over the period July 2022 through April 2026. All models are assessed under a purged walk-forward backtesting framework. The naive linear model (Model A), which contains no estimated parameters and serves as an honest alpha detector, produces a mean Rank Information Coefficient of-0.0097 (t =-1.54) and a net Sharpe ratio of-3.22. The orthogonal linear model (Model B) yields nearly identical results (IC =-0.0102, t =-1.61). The gradient-boosted ranker (Model C) achieves a weakly positive IC of +0.0243 (t = 3.55), yet still destroys capital (net Sharpe =-2.91, maximum drawdown =-95.6%). The evidence compels rejection of the hypothesis that the employed OHLCV and funding rate signals contain exploitable crosssectional alpha for large-cap crypto perpetual futures at an eight-hour horizon. The paper documents the failure transparently, dissects its likely causes, and derives actionable lessons for future research.</jats:p>
